rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Triliteral verbs expanded to quadriliteral patterns take matching verbal-noun patterns, as with jalbaba/jalbaba and shamlala/shamlala.
rows.anchor: على ذلك أن المصدر كالمصدر من بنات الأربعة نحو جلببت جلببة وشمللت شمللة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These expanded forms may also take initial tāʾ to form derivatives such as taqallasā and tashayṭana, with corresponding verbal nouns.
rows.anchor: التاء في أوائلها كما لحقت في تدحرج وذلك قولك قلسيته فتقلسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inserted nūn occurs only with specified augmented triliterals, including forms whose extra element is at the lām position or final yāʾ; their inflection follows istifʿala.
rows.anchor: ولم تزد هذه النون في هذه الأشياء إلا فيما كانت الزيادة فيه من

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh treats the listed augmented triliteral patterns as the full inventory; anything beyond them is not Arabic usage, and he gives their verbal nouns and distributions.
rows.anchor: ما جاوز هذه الأمثلة فليس من كلام العرب وبينت مصادرهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamza, yāʾ, tāʾ, and nūn uniquely prefix verbs, including unaugmented and augmented forms, when the action is non-past.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك أفعل ويفعل ونفعل وتفعل وقد بين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some augment positions are shared across noun and verb patterns while others are not: yāʾ occurs in the cited fourth-position forms where wāw, tāʾ, and mīm do not.
rows.anchor: وتقول أفعل نحو أفكل فالياء تلحق رابعة والواو لا تلحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To identify shared augment positions, compare the number of letters and the position of the added element; unshared forms are recognized by departing from that position.
rows.anchor: الذي عنيت في الشركة فتفطن له فإنه يتبين في الفصول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the interrogative hamza, a fronted object is accusative through an understood verb reconstructed from the clause; accusative is the preferred, standard construction.
rows.anchor: تقول أعبد الله ضربته وأزيدا مررت به وأعمرا قتلت أخاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted verb has the same interpretation as the overt explanatory verb used in comparable noninterrogative fronting.
rows.anchor: ففي كل هذا قد أضمرت بين الألف والاسم فعلا هذا تفسيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the clause subject is related to the fronted noun, that subject's nominative case makes the fronted noun nominative; an unrelated object instead takes accusative.
rows.anchor: فاعل والذى ليس من سببه مفعول فيرتفع إذا ارتفع الذى من سببه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the related noun is made the object and another noun the subject, the initial noun becomes accusative, as in the switch from Zayd as subject to his brother as object.
rows.anchor: فإن جعلت زيدا الفاعل قلت أعبد الله ضرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fronted noun with a following prepositional phrase is case-marked as though the verb governed it directly; removing the phrase reveals the accusative pattern.
rows.anchor: وتقول آلسوط ضرب به زيد وهو كقولك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fronted noun followed by a passive or intransitive verb plus a preposition must be nominative when the clause without that phrase is nominative.
rows.anchor: أزيد انطلق ms046 به لم يكن إلا رفعا لأنك لو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted word retains the case governance it would have if expressed, whether genitive, accusative, or nominative.
rows.anchor: وإذا أعملت العرب شيئا مضمرا لم يخرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the interrogative hamza falls on a pronoun starting a new clause, nominative is ordinary, though accusative fronting remains good Arabic.
rows.anchor: وتقول أأنت عبد الله ضربته تجريه ها هنا مجرى أنا زيد ضربته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A time adverb does not separate the interrogative from the object: the object remains accusative when fronted before a verb followed by an adverbial phrase.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت أكل يوم زيدا تضربه فهو نصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A clause beginning with a noun related to the fronted noun can be parsed like a new nominal clause; making that related noun an object licenses accusative on the initial noun.
rows.anchor: أعبد الله أخوه تضربه كما تقول أأنت زيد ضربته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raising is also possible in forms such as a fronted noun with a prepositional verb, and is stronger with marartu bihi than with a direct object construction because the initial noun can be a topic.
rows.anchor: فكأنه قال أعبد الله أخوك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the fronted noun is analyzed as governed by the hidden verb, a verb requiring a preposition should make it genitive; overt and understood words otherwise share their governance.
rows.anchor: فمن زعم ms047 أنه إذا قال أزيدا مررت به إنما ينصبه بهذا الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In conditional senses, ḥaythu and idhā make a following noun accusative when a verb follows, but allow a nominative noun when followed by a nominal predicate.
rows.anchor: نصبا فى القياس إذا وحيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idh permits an initial nominative noun, especially with a present-tense predicate; a past-tense predicate is awkward because idh is used in obligatory narrative contexts.
rows.anchor: وأما إذ فيحسن ابتداء الاسم بعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fronted noun is accusative when the later coordinated phrase is semantically connected to it, as through a shared description; without that connection, the construction is not valid.
rows.anchor: ومما ينتصب أوله لأن آخره ملتبس بالأول قوله أزيدا ضربت عمرا وأخاه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Active participles such as ḍārib and munzil operate like finite verbs, allowing arguments to precede them and allowing arguments to be expressed or understood.
rows.anchor: كأنك قلت أنت ضارب وأنت مكرم وأنت نازل كما كان ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Plural active participles on fawāʿil behave like feminine singular participles; Sībawayh cites Abū Kabīr's ʿawāqid and al-Aʿajjāj's awālif.
rows.anchor: هن حواج بيت الله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some speakers treat faʿʿāl as equivalent to fawʿal in plural usage, as in qaṭṭān of Mecca and sukkān of the Sacred Territory.
rows.anchor: بعضهم فعالا بمنزلة فوعل فقالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intensive agent forms operate like fāʿil when they convey an intensified action; common patterns include faʿūl, faʿʿāl, mifʿāl, and fiʿl.
rows.anchor: أكثر هذا المعنى فعول وفعال ومفعال وفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿīl forms such as raḥīm, ʿalīm, qadīr, samīʿ, and baṣīr can share fāʿil's argument order and omission patterns.
rows.anchor: كرحيم وعليم وقدير وسميع وبصير يجوز فيهن ما جاز فى فاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poems by Dhū al-Rumma, Abū Dhuʾayb, and al-Qilākh show intensive participles such as هجّوم, هيوج, and لبّاس taking the flexible syntax of fāʿil.
rows.anchor: هجوم عليها نفسه غير أنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spoken phrase أما العسل فأنا شراب and poems with ḍarūb, including a line by Abū Ṭālib, further attest intensive forms used like active participles.
rows.anchor: من يقول أما العسل فأنا شراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fiʿl pattern is much rarer than faʿīl; ʿAmr ibn Aḥmar's misḥal is one poetic example.
rows.anchor: أو مسحل شنج عضادة سمحج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh adduces forms from Ṭarafa, an unnamed poet, Ruʾbah, Sāʿidah ibn Juʾayyah, and al-Kumayt as further examples of intensive fiʿl forms.
rows.anchor: برأس دماغ رءوس العز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verbal intensives differ from nominal descriptions such as ḥasan wajh al-akh: the latter cannot be inverted, pronominalized, or split like an operative participle.
rows.anchor: حسن وجه الأخ لأن هذا لا يقلب ولا يضمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verbal nouns can govern like verbs; Sībawayh cites the lines with يمررون, ندل, and ضرب to show verbal nouns taking verbal arguments.
rows.anchor: فندلا زريق المال ندل الثعالب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names such as rasūl, ʿadīl, jalīs, and amīr are not action-intensifying participles, so a preceding interrogative noun remains nominative.
rows.anchor: رسول له ورسوله لأنك لا تريد بفعول ههنا ما تريد به فى ضروب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A time expression with a nonverbal title such as amīr is nominative, unlike the same adverb before an operative verb; it is not governed by an action.
rows.anchor: أنت فيه أمير ترفعه لأنه ليس بفاعل وقد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A verbal noun such as ḍarb Zaydan means an understood finite clause; unlike an active participle, it does not state its agent, so agent and object may both need expression.
rows.anchor: وإنما خالف هذا الاسم الذى جرى مجرى الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾanic infinitive iṭʿām governs the object yatīman, illustrating the verbal noun's ability to take an object.
rows.anchor: في يوم ذي مسغبة يتيما ذا مقربة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With tanwīn, a verbal noun can take overt agent and patient nouns in either role, corresponding to an understood finite clause.
rows.anchor: أنه يضرب زيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If tanwīn is omitted, the following noun is genitive and substitutes for it; that noun may represent either the verbal noun's agent or its object.
rows.anchor: ويصير المجرور بدلا من التنوين معاقبا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A verbal noun can coordinate agent and patient nouns as an active participle does; Ruʾbah's lines illustrate this governing construction.
rows.anchor: كما فعلت ذلك فى الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the definite article, the verbal noun can govern an accusative object like an active participle; Sībawayh cites poetry including a line by al-Murār al-Asadī.
rows.anchor: وتقول عجبت من الضرب زيدا كما قلت عجبت من

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh rejects الضرب الرجل as nonstandard because it resembles an adjectival phrase; al-Khalīl accepts a broader construction by analogy with ḥasan al-akh.
rows.anchor: الحسن الأخ والحسن وجه الأخ

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl accepts by analogy a verbal-noun construction modeled on the adjectival phrase, though Sībawayh says this is not ordinary speech.
rows.anchor: وكان الخليل يراه | وإن شئت قلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unarticled verbal noun may be annexed with or without tanwīn, whether the action actually occurred or not.
rows.anchor: ويكون منونا وليس بمنزلة ضارب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A verbal noun can take a time adverb, as in عجبت من ضرب اليوم زيدا; poetry contrasts this with اليوم in a nonverbal nominal phrase.
rows.anchor: يا سارق الليلة أهل الدار
